title: Processions
hook: Holy Week in Seville, Corpus Christi in villages: faith in the streets

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Day of the Dead: a photograph, a candle, marigolds in a path to the door. Your line was they're remembered. Whose face did you set out? Day one thousand four hundred one.

Late at night in a narrow street in Seville, during Holy Week. The crowd is packed so tight nobody can turn around. Then a drum, slow, and a hush. Around the corner comes a huge wooden platform, swaying gently, lit by rows of candles, carrying a figure of Christ bent under his cross. Nobody can see who carries it. The bearers are hidden underneath, shoulders to the beams, moving in step to a voice calling from outside. In front walk long lines of penitents in robes and tall pointed hoods, holding candles. A woman on a balcony sings a short, raw song to the figure as it passes. Today, processions.
screen: `LATE AT NIGHT IN SEVILLE.` → `A PLATFORM CARRIED BY HIDDEN BEARERS.` → `A SONG FROM A BALCONY.`

segments.voice: Start in the Gospels, with a crowd on a road. As Jesus rides into Jerusalem, people spread their cloaks on the road and cut branches from the trees, and they walk ahead and behind him, shouting. In the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." On Palm Sunday, Catholics repeat that walk with branches in their hands. A procession is faith that moves. Next, Seville. In Holy Week its brotherhoods, lay associations of Catholics, carry images of Christ and of Mary through the streets. The pointed hoods are penitents' hoods. Tradition says they hide the face so the penance is offered without anyone knowing who is doing it. The bearers underneath are hidden too. The whole thing is built so that the images are seen and the people aren't. Then a quieter scene. On Corpus Christi, the priest carries the Eucharist in a monstrance, under a canopy, through the streets of a parish or a village. In some villages people lay carpets of flower petals and colored sawdust for it to pass over, carpets that are trampled in minutes. Church law asks for a public procession on this feast where it can be done, as a public witness of reverence. Last, why walk at all. A church building holds faith still. A procession takes it out the door, past the bakery and the bus stop, and says, without a sermon, that God isn't only indoors. It also says that the Church is a people on the move, walking somewhere together.
screen: `HOSANNA ON THE ROAD.` · `SEVILLE: HIDDEN FACES, SEEN IMAGES.` · `CORPUS CHRISTI OVER FLOWER CARPETS.` · `GOD ISN'T ONLY INDOORS.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk and pray outdoors, even briefly. If you can, stand up and step outside, or walk to a window. Settle, and breathe. Notice the street: who passes, what's open, what you hear. Then take a few slow steps, as if you were in a procession, unhurried, in step with your breath. If you pray, you can say the Hosanna line quietly as you walk, or carry someone in your prayer. If you don't, carry a good wish for the people you see, one by one. If you can't move today, let your eyes do the walking. The bell holds the time.
Processions. The Church walking together through the streets with branches, images or the Eucharist: on Palm Sunday, in Holy Week, on Corpus Christi. Today's word.

Your line: faith in the streets. Today, the next time you go out your door, carry one name or one good wish with you all the way there and back, like a small procession of one. Day one thousand four hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholics walk in procession with palms on Palm Sunday and, in some places, follow the Eucharist through the streets on Corpus Christi. In Seville and elsewhere in Spain, lay brotherhoods carry images of Christ and Mary through the streets during Holy Week.

fork.setup: you're a bearer under a Holy Week platform in Seville. the crowd outside can't see you. why is it built that way?
options: so nobody can take credit: the images are seen, the people aren't.
because the bearers are not allowed to watch the procession.
to keep the platform's weight secret.
fork.reveal: the bearers underneath and the hooded penitents in front are hidden alike. the whole procession is arranged so the images are seen, and the people aren't.

Canon 944 §1 paraphrased: where it can be done in the judgment of the diocesan bishop, a procession through the public streets is to be held, especially on Corpus Christi, as a public witness of veneration toward the Eucharist. Confirm.

Seville: brotherhoods (hermandades/cofradías), hidden bearers (costaleros) under the pasos, hooded penitents (nazarenos), and the saeta sung from a balcony are described without names, dates or numbers.
The hood's meaning (anonymity in penance) is the standard explanation; confirm. The script makes no reference to unrelated uses of similar hoods elsewhere.
Flower and sawdust carpets for Corpus Christi are described as 'in some villages'.
Original: Greek Ὡσαννά, transliterating a Hebrew/Aramaic cry; confirm accent and pronunciation.
Editor pass: cut the unsourced route 'to the cathedral and back'; put the hood's meaning as tradition; replaced the carry's walk-to-the-car/bus image, which repeated day 1384.
